prize_parts.citation: For the invention of the optical lattice clock and its development to the 10^-18 level of uncertainty, opening a new regime of precision measurement

statement.case_for: I have changed my preferred configuration from the Higgs discovery (B056) to the optical lattice clock (B008), and I want to be plain about why. My view of the science has not moved: the Higgs is the larger result about nature and the experimental half is still unrecognised. What moved me is that, after a full round, nobody including me can state a rule that picks three of Gianotti, Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee without an arbitrary cut. Pearce asked for a principled criterion and I do not have one; spokesperson titles do not reliably track who did the original work, as Olsson says. A prize I cannot defend on the record is a prize I should not propose. B008 meets my own test of finding clues in nature: lattice clocks are independently reproduced and surpassed in Sr, Yb and Hg systems and compared routinely across continents, so the measurement is not in question. Katori's magic-wavelength lattice is a single identifiable idea, and Ye's group took it to the 10^-18 level and showed the many-body and spin-exchange physics behind it. Two names match two identifiable steps. The citation should rest only on what has been demonstrated, namely the invention and the realisation at 10^-18, and not on constants, geodesy or dark matter, which are prospective. That also answers the chair's overlap question: the comb of 2005 and the ion control of 2012 provide the readout and the quantum-control foundations, but not the neutral-atom lattice with many atoms and no first-order light shift, which is a different idea.
statement.case_against: I still think the clock is a superb new capability rather than a discovery, and I do not want to hide that. No deviation from standard physics has been found, so its reach into physics beyond the standard model is a promise. The SI second is not yet redefined, though I agree with the five colleagues who say that should not be a precondition. Attribution also has edges: Lemonde, Ludlow, Sterr, Gill and the NIST, PTB and SYRTE groups are outside the pair, and I cannot say from the supplied material whether any key systematic, such as the blackbody shift or hyperpolarisability, was settled by someone else. If Lindroth or Kroll can show that one was, the citation must say invention and development, and not clocks in general. The Higgs and topological insulators both remain stronger types of achievement in my view, and I would not call B008 a certain choice if either attribution problem were solved.

responses.point: Pearce asks whether there is a principled rule (for example spokespersons at discovery) for choosing three of the four ATLAS and CMS leaders, and says he would rather not make the Higgs the first choice unless one is found.
responses.response: I tried to build that rule and could not. Spokespersons at the time of discovery would give Gianotti and Incandela, and Incandela is not among the credited names. Founding spokespersons give Jenni, Della Negra and Virdee, and drop Gianotti, who led ATLAS when the discovery was announced. Any rule that gets to Gianotti, Jenni and Virdee is chosen to produce that trio. You are right that three people from four is a judgement and not a result, and that is the reason I am withdrawing B056 as my first choice, not any doubt about its science.

responses.point: Lindroth says the uncertainty budgets of the lattice clock are credible from her own systematic-shift and atomic-structure calculations, and that the merit of B056 is not in dispute but its attribution is.
responses.response: Your judgement on the uncertainty budgets is what I lack, and it matters to me, because a clock can look clean in a press release and still rest on a shaky systematic. I take it that the 10^-18 claims are credible and have been reproduced, which is what I asked for in my own first-round reply. I would ask you to answer the chair's question directly: did any key shift, the lattice light shift, blackbody or density shift, get pinned down by a group outside Katori and Ye? If so, the citation must be worded around the lattice invention and its realisation, so that the credit boundary is honest.

responses.point: Eriksson argues that Kane and Mele's Z2 and quantum spin Hall concept plus Molenkamp's experiment is a complete core, and that the 3D story can be treated as later.
responses.response: I find a new state of matter an appealing kind of result, and in kind it is closer to a discovery about nature than the clock is, which is why B049 stays among my alternatives. I still cannot square the lineage. Mehlig, Johansson, Lindroth and Olsson all say the HgTe experiment tested the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal, not the Kane-Mele graphene model, and Zhang's death means the omission cannot be repaired later. The word 'complete' needs an argument that the experiment would have been done without the proposal. I have not heard that one yet, and I would not vote for a citation that skips the step that made the experiment possible.

responses.point: Kroll notes that the credit could be argued as Katori's alone, with Ye's contribution being performance rather than concept, and that the citation must state the invention and its realisation at 10^-18. He also discloses a year in John Hall's laboratory.
responses.response: I agree on the wording and would defend naming both the invention and the development, since the second half is what turned a good idea into the measurement everyone now compares against. On the disclosure, a year in Hall's laboratory during a PhD and no collaboration with Katori or Ye is, in my view, a disclosed field proximity and not a reason to recuse. Whether you take part in the final ballot is the committee's call, and I would be content for it to be recorded, with five other members available to outvote any bias.

uncertainties: Whether a key lattice-clock systematic was established outside Katori and Ye, which would change the credit boundary and the citation wording.

Whether the committee prefers a measurement capability to a discovery about nature when the attribution is cleaner for the former; I am not fully at ease with the choice and am not certain it is right.
Whether a defensible rule for the ATLAS and CMS trio exists; I could not find one, but a colleague with more knowledge of the collaborations may.
Whether the overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes will be read as a new idea or as a refinement of a rewarded line.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for any shortlisted candidate. My work in string theory and cosmology is remote from every shortlisted field, and I have no tie to Katori, Ye, or the ATLAS and CMS leaders. My former supervisor, David Gross, is not connected to any shortlisted candidate.
